title: The other four precepts
hookLine: a borrowed charger nobody would call stolen, and the precept still notices
tomorrow: a wish for all beings: should you start with yourself?

cards: Your coworker's phone charger, borrowed off her desk without asking, back by lunch. Nobody in the office would call that stealing. The second precept, though, never uses a word for stealing at all.
It says adinnadana. Adinna: not given. Adana: taking.
Taking the not-given. That's the answer to yesterday's question, and it's a stranger line than theft: not was it stolen, but was it given? The charger wasn't.

teach.b: Each of the other three has a key word worth holding. The third: kamesu micchacara, wrong conduct in sensual pleasures. Teachers usually take it to mean sexual conduct that harms or betrays someone.
Musa, false; vada, speech. False speech. Not only the big lie, but any word you know isn't true.

In one sutta the Buddha shows his young son Rahula a water dipper with a little water left in it, tosses the water out, and says that is how empty the practice of someone becomes who feels no shame in a deliberate lie.
And the fifth has the strangest wording of all. It doesn't just say alcohol.

It names drinks and drugs, and then adds pamada-tthana: a ground for heedlessness. The rule carries its own reason inside it. What it points at is the losing of care, the moment the mind stops minding.

teach.h: LINES DRAWN WIDER THAN THE LAW.
teach.b: So here's the puzzle, solved: the precepts keep drawing their lines a little wider than the law does. Not stolen, but not given. Not just lies under oath, but false speech.
Not one drink, but whatever makes you careless. All five end the same way: veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training to refrain.

how: In Theravada temples, lay people chant the five precepts in Pali, a monk leading each line and everyone repeating it, and some recite them at home as well.

games.q: what does “the other four precepts” mean?
o: the not-given, desire, false speech, heedlessness
the four meals a monk may eat in a day
four temple duties that lay people share

games.q: the key words — tap the pairs.

s: the second precept only covers what the law calls stealing
its word is adinnadana, taking the not-given: the line is whether it was given.
the fifth precept names its own reason
it calls drinks and drugs a ground for heedlessness, pamada.

games.q: your cousin says the fifth precept just means alcohol is evil. what does its wording actually point at?
o: drinks and drugs as a ground for heedlessness: the losing of care.
the taste of alcohol itself, which the precept calls a sin.
drinking only on temple grounds; elsewhere it doesn't apply.
games.why: the fifth precept adds pamada-tthana, a ground for heedlessness. the rule carries its reason: what it guards is the mind's care.

practice: Chant the five slowly, each ending veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. Then pick the one that will be hardest this week, name the moment it's likely to slip, and choose one small move for that moment. Sit with the plan until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The other four precepts. The not-given, harm in desire, false speech, and the ground for heedlessness. Word eleven of a little Pali.

orig.note: adinnadana in Devanagari letters: taking (adana) the not-given (adinna).

carryVoice: Something to carry: five trainings, each line drawn a little wider than you'd expect. That's eleven.

sources.ref: The five precepts (pañcasīla): adinnādānā, kāmesu micchācārā, musāvādā, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi
sources.work: Theravada chanting (the five precepts); compare Khuddakapatha 2
